findings.heading: Versions of `NA`
findings.proposition: English names the dplyr function as `case_when()`, which is what the code chunk below uses; the Turkish names it `case_while()` (and links to anchor `#clean_case_while`).
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader searching for or typing `case_while()` finds no such dplyr function and gets an 'object not found' error; the cross-reference link also points at a non-existent anchor.

findings.heading: Versions of `NA`
findings.proposition: English says the NA variants are unlikely to be met unless you use `case_when()` to create a new column; the Turkish says `case_while()`.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the rule applies to a function that does not exist, so cannot connect the NA_real_/NA_character_ guidance to the real `case_when()` they will actually write.

findings.heading: "Shadow" columns
findings.proposition: English says the shadow columns are used to STRATIFY a statistical summary; the Turkish says only that they can be used to CREATE a statistical summary.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the point of the example: that `group_by(date_outcome_NA)` splits the summary by missingness. They may read the chunk as an ordinary summary and miss the missingness comparison it is making.

findings.heading: Types of missing data
findings.proposition: English says the chills-and-aches information could be used to IMPUTE the missing data; the Turkish says it could be used to ASSESS ('degerlendirmek') the missing data.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is given an assessment example where the English gives the worked motivation for imputation under MAR, weakening the link between MAR and why imputation is possible.

findings.heading: Types of missing data
findings.proposition: English advises collecting more data about why data are missing RATHER THAN ATTEMPTING TO IMPUTE under MNAR; the Turkish drops the 'rather than attempt to impute it' clause.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader facing MNAR data does not receive the explicit warning against imputing it, and may go on to apply the mice methods taught later in the chapter to data where the chapter says they should not.

findings.heading: Imputation
findings.proposition: English says it is probably unreasonable to drop every variable that has A LOT OF MISSING DATA; the Turkish says every variable that has 'too much data' ('cok fazla verisi olan'), dropping the word missing.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence states a rule about variables with plenty of data, which is the opposite population, so the reader gets no guidance about the variables the paragraph is actually about.

findings.heading: Useful packages
findings.proposition: English introduces the chunk as loading the `mice` package; the Turkish calls it the 'Fare' package (Turkish for the animal mouse), while the chunk runs `pacman::p_load(mice)`.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader who takes 'Fare' as the package name will try to install a package that does not exist, and cannot match the prose to the `mice` in the chunk beside it.

findings.heading: Regression imputation
findings.proposition: English says that even with a very good model the variability of imputed data may be UNDERESTIMATED; the Turkish says only that the variability may not be well estimated, dropping the direction of the error.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader loses the specific, actionable warning that single regression imputation biases variance downward, so will not know that standard errors and confidence intervals from such data are too narrow.

findings.heading: LOCF and BOCF
findings.proposition: English defines LOCF and BOCF as IMPUTATION methods for time series/longitudinal data; the Turkish calls them assessment/evaluation methods ('degerlendirme yontemleri').
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader may file LOCF and BOCF under missingness assessment rather than imputation, and not recognise them as alternatives to the mean, regression and multiple imputation methods in the surrounding sections.

findings.heading: LOCF and BOCF
findings.proposition: English says the missing year values for quarters after Q1 will need to be IMPUTED; the Turkish says they will need to be COUNTED ('saymamiz gerekecek').
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the demonstration is about counting missing years, so does not see that the `fill(year)` chunk that follows is performing the imputation the sentence set up.

findings.heading: Multiple Imputation
findings.proposition: English says the mice package CAN TAKE CARE OF many of the modelling details for you; the Turkish says you MUST PAY ATTENTION TO the modelling details of the mice package.
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader is told the opposite of the English reassurance, and may conclude that multiple imputation with mice demands manual specification of the modelling details that mice in fact handles by default.

findings.heading: Multiple Imputation
findings.proposition: English says there are many details it has GLOSSED OVER; the Turkish says there are many details it has DWELT ON ('Uzerinde durdugumuz birçok ayrinti').
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish reader does not learn that the section is a simplified summary, so may treat what they have read as complete coverage of multiple imputation and not consult the referenced book for the omitted detail.

findings.heading: Multiple Imputation
findings.proposition: English recommends multiple imputation because it ISN'T ALWAYS MUCH MORE WORK than a complete case analysis; the Turkish says it is NEVER MORE USEFUL than a complete case analysis ('her zaman tam bir vaka analizi yapmaktan daha fazla ise yaramaz').
findings.reader_consequence: The Turkish sentence ends the chapter by telling the reader multiple imputation gains them nothing over complete case analysis, which reverses the chapter's recommendation and would lead them to skip imputation entirely.
